title: Quran Study 67: Capital Punishment, Wills, Inheritance, and Adoption (1982-12-10)

cases.question: How did Rashad interpret the categories in Quran 2:178?
cases.expected_answer_note: Rashad rejects killing an innocent person of the same category and interprets the categories of free, enslaved, male, and female as excuses to avoid execution when killer and victim differ. The law sets a maximum of one life for one life, favors pardon and compensation, and is called life-saving.

cases.question: Why did the wrongful-execution example matter?
cases.expected_answer_note: A recent lethal injection and the possibility of executing the wrong person are used to argue for reversible compensation rather than death. Rashad says the victim or the victim's kin acts as judge within a fixed maximum and cites Quran 5:45's soul-for-soul rule. Participants note that this interpretation differs from prevailing practice.

cases.question: What duties concerning wills appear in Quran 2:180–182?
cases.expected_answer_note: Latifa reads the command to dictate a will for parents and relatives, the sin of altering a witnessed will, and the permission to correct obvious sinful partiality. Rashad says Quranic law is not rigid when an alteration restores justice.

cases.question: How were unequal shares connected with financial obligations?
cases.expected_answer_note: Dean and Rashad discuss Quranic shares for sons, daughters, wives, and other relatives alongside men's financial obligations. They say a will cannot arbitrarily dispossess protected family members, debate a son who attempted to kill his father, and distinguish fixed inheritance from household objects or ongoing support for poor families, schools, mosques, or churches that must be documented.

cases.question: How did Rashad treat adopted children in inheritance?
cases.expected_answer_note: Rashad says adopted children are members of the family and should receive equal treatment while retaining their original lineage names. He also rejects disinheriting children because they are Jewish, Christian, or otherwise outside the parent's religion. Dean describes Southeast Asian and Philippine customs excluding adopted children and interfaith relatives, a wealthy family fearing loss of an estate, and the possibility of transferring property as a lifetime gift.
